describes: Modal-head phrases the prose grammar's modal_head production recognises, each mapped to one of the three canonical lexemes (shall/must/may) the truth table (_NEGATED_MODAL in deontic.prose_grammar) dispatches on. A data table, not a regex: the recursive-descent parser matches a phrase's words at a token position; it does not compile or search a pattern. Multi-word phrases are tried longest-first at each position. An entry may also carry a literal 'operator' (Phase 1 scope: F for 'is prohibited from'/'is not permitted to', P for 'is authorised to'): the phrase itself already lexicalises a modal (a negated one, for the F entries), so the grammar dispatches straight to that operator instead of through the lexeme/negation table. An entry that carries a literal 'operator' may also carry 'negates': true when the phrase's own wording is itself a negator ('is prohibited from', 'is not permitted to' lexicalise a negated modal) that must be counted alongside any adverb/determiner/interposed negator when the grammar decides AMBIGUOUS_NEGATION (deontic.prose_grammar.analyze); omitted/false for a forced operator phrase that carries no negation of its own ('is authorised to' forces P without negating anything). English only (Phase 1 scope). The permission modal cues did not originally carry the 'shall be' forms real EU legislation uses alongside the bare 'is'/'are' forms: DSA Art. 60(4) 'the Digital Services Coordinator ... shall be entitled to ...', GDPR Art. 12(8) 'the Commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts ...'. 'shall be entitled to'/'are entitled to'/'shall be empowered to'/'shall be authorised to'/'shall be authorized to'/'shall have the power to' are mapped to the plain lexeme 'may' (no forced operator), the same route 'is entitled to' already takes: longest-match-first at the modal_head's own start position already prefers e.g. 'shall be entitled to' over the bare 'shall' at the same token, so the bare obligation lexeme never wins once the longer phrase is published here — no separate ordering rule is needed beyond that existing longest-first dispatch. Routing through the lexeme table rather than a forced operator (unlike 'is authorised to') also keeps a genuine trailing negator ('shall never, in any circumstances, be entitled to ...') dispatching through the same (lexeme, negated) truth table instead of being silently ignored by a forced P. Each of these six carries 'requires_verb_complement': true: the modal_head production only accepts the match when the word right after it is, case-insensitively, a member of the closed POSITIVE verb list published in artifacts/gazetteer/complement_verbs.json (see that file's own describes field for the list and its corpus-derived provenance) — not a negative filter trying to recognise everything that is NOT a verb phrase. A determiner/demonstrative/clause-marker lead ('shall be authorised to THE EXTENT that ...'), a bare noun or adjective complement ('are entitled to COMPENSATION', 'shall be entitled to FAIR compensation', 'shall be entitled to LEGAL aid', 'shall be entitled to PAID annual leave', 'shall be entitled to EQUAL treatment'), a gerund ('shall be entitled to RECEIVING compensation' — 'receiving' is not the bare verb form 'receive'), and a possessive lead ('shall have the power to ITS own investigative powers') are all rejected by the SAME single check, because none of them is spelled exactly like a listed base-form verb — not by several different negative rules trying to anticipate every such shape. A single bare verb is enough on its own ('shall have the power to INTERVENE.', 'are entitled to OBJECT.'): no minimum complement length is imposed, since 'intervene'/'object' are themselves listed verbs. complement_verbs.json's own 'noun_markers'/'verb_specific_noun_markers' are a SECOND, additive check examined only after the first word already passed the verb-list check: a listed verb immediately followed by 'of'/'for' ('entitled to TRANSFER OF the data', 'entitled to CHARGE OF the case') or, for 'access' specifically, by 'to' ('entitled to ACCESS TO the file') is the signature of that word's NOUN reading, not its verb one, and is rejected the same way. On a rejected match, five of the six entries fall back to the shorter 'shall'/no-match alternative at the same position, which then abstains on its own terms exactly as it did before these phrases existed (the remaining text opens on 'be', already a state_action_prefixes entry) — the gate never produces a NEW accepted frame for these five when the verb check fails; it only ever removes one. 'shall have the power to' is the one exception, and carries 'abstain_if_no_verb_complement': true for this reason: its own fallback ('shall' alone, remaining text opening on 'have', NOT a state_action_prefixes entry) would otherwise reach an accepted O/duty reading instead of abstaining ('The authority shall have the power to audit the controller.', 'The Lead Overseer shall have the power to:' must abstain, not read as a duty to 'have the power to audit'/'have the power to'); the flag makes the WHOLE modal_head search at this position fail outright (no further ranked alternative is tried) rather than fall through to that wrong reading. The pre-existing 'is entitled to'/'is authorised to' entries are left exactly as they were (no 'requires_verb_complement'): changing their already-relied-on behaviour is out of scope here. Hohfeldian incident is a separate layer (deontic.incidents.classify_incident): 'entitled to' carries no power-verb cue of its own and defaults to privilege; 'empowered to' is a power cue (deontic.incidents._POWER_VERBS carries the explicit 'empower'/'empowers'/'empowered'/'empowering' verb forms); 'authorised to'/'authorized to' already match that same regex's existing authoris/authoriz verb forms; 'have the power to' is itself a power cue in _POWER_VERBS ('(?:have|has) the power to'), so 'shall have the power to' reads as a power regardless of which verb follows it (adopt, order, impose, require, ...), not only when that verb happens to be an active 'require'.
